newsitem.title: USA: Retailers face executive, management shortage.
newsitem.headline: Retailers face executive, management shortage.

text.p: The retailing industry, which has been revamped by mergers and cost-cutting, faces a shortage of qualified managers and executives in today's healthy job market, industry analysts say.
The shortage is acute at major chains, they say, with the lack of experienced managers showing up in poor merchandising and bland store appearances.

Dillon Read retailing analyst Peter Schaeffer said several factors have led to the dearth of talented retailing executives, including cutbacks in recruiting and training, shrinking company loyalty and a loss of many perks such as travel that these jobs once offered.

Sears, Roebuck and Co. Director of College Relations Bob Wery said smaller graduating classes, a low unemployment rate and a negative view among college graduates toward retailing jobs have all contributed to the difficulty of bringing in new talent.
In addition, salaries at most retailers tend to lag behind other fields.
Kerson said graduates could earn $80,000 to $90,000 out of business school as a retailing executive, but the best students gravitate toward Wall Street, lured by the prospect of fatter paychecks.
At Sears, starting salaries for college graduate management trainees range from $25,600 to $28,200, in line with other big retailers in the industry, Wery said.

"Retail in general is one of the industries (that has) not invested in people and viewed them as costs that need to be cut," said Tony Rucci, executive vice president of administration at Sears. Training is usually one of the first places to be cut, he said.
"When Macy's, A&S and Bloomingdales were running, they were able to produce 500 executives a year," said Robert Kerson, chairman of the executive search firm Levy Kerson.
Abraham & Strauss closed its doors in 1995, while Macy's and Bloomingdale's have been acquired by Federated Department Stores.

"Federated is regarded as training ground for retailing executives," said David Clark, Federated's vice president of organizational development. Clark declined to say what Federated spends on training, but said the amount has increased in the past few years.
Clark acknowledged that consolidation has resulted in the need for "more sophisticated leaders and executives" since regional chains have become national operations.
Bud Wright, a principal search consultant at the Lemming LeVan executive search firm, said an increasing number of retailers have had to look outside retailing to fill key jobs.

"Retailing is a victim of its own visibility," said Steve Kirn, Sears and Roebuck Co.'s vice president of education and development. "People experience just the front end of retailing. They don't see what's behind the sales associate in the store."

Wery said the industry has been seeking to recruit better managers by improving ties with universities, even holding a forum at Indiana University last month to bring together leading retailers and business professors.
But retailers need to "extol (the industry's) virtues and be more aggressive on college campuses," Kerson said.
While the pool of talented applicants may have narrowed, Federated's Clark said finding great managers has always been tough.
"There is never enough talent in any industry or any company," he said. We're always after good talent."
